subChunks.title: Building a Button Component
subChunks.hookHtml: The Button is the most fundamental interactive component in any UI system. Building it well requires applying everything from the Apprentice tier: spacing, colour, typography, borders, states, transitions, and accessibility. Get the button right and you understand how Tailwind's utilities compose into real production components.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Button anatomy

A production button needs classes for: size, colour, text, border, rounding, spacing, all interactive states, and accessibility:

/* Primary button — the most important action on the page */
.btn-primary {
  /* Layout */
  inline-flex items-center justify-center gap-2
  /* Sizing */
  px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium
  /* Appearance */
  bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-md
  /* States */
  hover:bg-blue-700
  active:scale-95
  focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 focus:ring-offset-2
  disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed
  /* Transition */
  transition-all duration-150
}

Button variants

/* Secondary — less prominent */
bg-white text-gray-700 border border-gray-300
hover:bg-gray-50 hover:text-gray-900

/* Destructive — dangerous action */
bg-red-600 text-white
hover:bg-red-700 focus:ring-red-500

/* Ghost — minimal, text-only look */
bg-transparent text-blue-600
hover:bg-blue-50

/* Link — looks like a link, behaves like a button */
bg-transparent text-blue-600 underline
hover:text-blue-800

Button sizes

/* Small */
px-3 py-1.5 text-xs font-medium rounded

/* Medium (default) */
px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium rounded-md

/* Large */
px-6 py-3 text-base font-semibold rounded-lg

/* Full width */
w-full flex items-center justify-center

Icon buttons

/* Icon + text */
<button class="inline-flex items-center gap-2 px-4 py-2...">
  <svg class="w-4 h-4">...</svg>
  Accept Quest
</button>

/* Icon only — needs accessible label */
<button class="p-2 rounded-md hover:bg-gray-100" aria-label="Delete quest">
  <svg class="w-5 h-5 text-gray-500">...</svg>
</button>

Loading state

<button class="... opacity-75 cursor-wait" disabled>
  <svg class="animate-spin w-4 h-4" ...>...</svg>
  Accepting...
</button>

Lyra: "inline-flex items-center justify-center is the correct display for buttons — it allows icon and text to align without extra span wrappers. Never use just flex on a button unless you want it to be full-width. The difference between a professional button library and an amateur one is whether loading, disabled, and focus states are all handled consistently."

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: A button seems simple. It is not. A real production button has five states: resting, hovered, active, focused, and disabled. It aligns icons and text correctly. It has a loading state. It communicates hierarchy — primary, secondary, destructive. Build a button that handles all of these, and you have built the foundation of a design system.

storyBeats.speaker: Button with all states — the production standard
storyBeats.text:
<button class="
  inline-flex items-center justify-center gap-2
  px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium rounded-md
  bg-blue-600 text-white
  hover:bg-blue-700
  active:scale-95
  focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 focus:ring-offset-2
  disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed
  transition-all duration-150
">
  Accept Quest
</button>

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a complete button suite. Each button must include all interactive states:

  • .btn-primary: blue background, white text, all five states (hover, active, focus ring, disabled, transition)
  • .btn-secondary: white background, gray-700 text, gray-300 border, hover:bg-gray-50
  • .btn-destructive: red-600 background, white text, hover:bg-red-700, focus:ring-red-500
  • .btn-ghost: transparent background, blue-600 text, hover:bg-blue-50
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a complete button component from scratch with five variants (primary, secondary, destructive, ghost, link), three sizes (sm, md, lg), a loading state with an animated spinner icon, and an icon-only variant with an aria-label. All buttons must have hover, active, focus, and disabled states.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through every class in a production primary button and explain what it does and why it is necessary. Which classes would a beginner typically forget, and what breaks without them? Explain why inline-flex items-center is preferred over just flex for buttons.

questions.prompt: A button contains an SVG icon and text. Which display utility correctly aligns them horizontally with a small gap?
options: inline-block with the SVG float: left
questions.explanation: inline-flex makes the button only as wide as its content (not full-width like flex). items-center aligns the icon and text vertically on the same baseline. gap-2 adds 8px of space between them. Using flex would make the button full-width, taking up an entire line.

questions.prompt: You have a destructive 'Delete Account' button. How should its appearance differ from a primary 'Save' button?
options: Red background (bg-red-600) instead of blue, with a red focus ring (focus:ring-red-500) to maintain semantic consistency
Gray background to de-emphasise the action
Identical to the primary button — the label communicates the danger
Outlined style only (border-red-600 text-red-600) so users don't click it accidentally
questions.answer: Red background (bg-red-600) instead of blue, with a red focus ring (focus:ring-red-500) to maintain semantic consistency
questions.explanation: Red is the universal UI convention for destructive or dangerous actions. The full class swap: bg-red-600 hover:bg-red-700 focus:ring-red-500. Everything else (padding, text size, font weight, transitions) stays the same — the only change is the colour, which communicates semantic meaning. The focus ring should also be red to maintain visual consistency for keyboard users.

questions.prompt: When should you use a ghost button variant versus a secondary button variant?
options: Ghost for tertiary actions in dense UIs where visual weight must be minimised (e.g., 'Cancel' in a dialog alongside a primary 'Confirm'). Secondary for less prominent actions that still need clear visual boundaries.
Ghost for dark backgrounds, secondary for light backgrounds
Ghost when the button has an icon, secondary when it has only text
They are interchangeable — both have lower visual weight than primary
questions.answer: Ghost for tertiary actions in dense UIs where visual weight must be minimised (e.g., 'Cancel' in a dialog alongside a primary 'Confirm'). Secondary for less prominent actions that still need clear visual boundaries.
questions.explanation: Secondary buttons have a visible border and background — they're clearly interactive but less prominent than primary. Ghost buttons have no background or border at rest — they look like text until hovered. Use secondary when you need two clear options at a similar level of importance. Use ghost when one option is significantly less important and you want to minimise its visual weight without making it hard to find.
